data.title: Jasenica – Predná Hôrka, a Púchov culture fort above the Váh
data.excerpt: Predná hôrka above Jasenica is one of the small forts of the Púchov culture that are scattered across north-western Slovakia. Surveys here yielded more than 60 metal objects, two brooches and a silver Celtic coin of the so-called Nitra type – the first of its kind with a certain find spot, which pushes the building of the fortification deeper into the 1st century BC.

data.metaDescription: A small Púchov culture fort above Jasenica in north-western Slovakia, where a silver Celtic coin of the Nitra type pushed its dating into the 1st century BC.

children.text: In one of the issues of the Vlastivedný zborník Povážia (Regional Studies Miscellany of the Váh Region) I came across a very interesting article about the Predná hôrka hillfort at Jasenica. Here I give an abridged version of it.

The territory of north-western Slovakia, delimited by the former districts of Čadca, Povážská Bystrica and Žilina, is literally interwoven with a multitude of sites that can be classed among fortified settlements. The largest number is represented by small fortifications on smaller prominent hills, which arose at the end of the Late Iron Age in the milieu of the Púchov culture. More than half of the fortifications known so far are dated, on the basis of the finds obtained, to the turn of the eras. Large fortifications – hillforts – are known only from the Late and Final Bronze Age, and some of them were used again in the period of the late La Tène up to the Early Roman period and then again in the 9th century AD (Divinka, Veľký vrch).

The small forts of the Púchov culture are distributed across the whole territory of north-western Slovakia and are among the most exposed positions of this region. They are mostly situated on small prominent hills, or at the end of larger, more extensive mountain ridges, in a range from 400 to 700 m above sea level.

The names of the individual sites are repeated quite often (Hrádek, Hrádok), but they are also known under the names Hôrka, Predná hôrka, or else Skala, Skalka, Mokrá skala, Štepnická skala, and sometimes after the owner of the land – Kulíškov kopec. The most surprising, however, is the name Zlatý kôň (Golden Horse) at Prosné, which is said to be so called because gold Celtic coins depicting a little horse were found here long ago

Several surveys have been carried out at the small fort of the Púchov culture at Jasenica. But the very first was the survey by A. Petrovský-Šichman as early as 1947. A few small sherds were then found on the southern slope of the hill of Predná hôrka. An important impulse for assigning the fortification to the framework of the Púchov culture, however, came only with the find of pottery made on 20 April 1958 by Štefan Meliš, who had gone with his wife from Papradno to look at the filling of the Nosice reservoir (the Reservoir of Youth). On the way he noticed a strange, prominent knoll on the Jasenica–Udiča route. He boasted of his discovery to the then specialist of the Povážské Museum in Žilina, A. Petrovský-Šichman, who set out with him once more to carry out a survey at this interesting site (Petrovský 1965, 69). Thus Predná hôrka came to the attention not only of specialists – archaeologists – but also of amateurs, who tried to find here finds that they might turn into money.

children.text: The further fate of the site was foreshadowed by chance digs, which it was possible to verify in 1979 as well, when a dug trench measuring 2 x 2 m was found on the northern terrace of the fortification. In its widened part not only small iron objects came to light, but above all almost complete vessels, including large storage jars, and also two stone querns. Yet the extent of the small fort gave no indication at all that such a quantity of antiquities would be found here. A repeated survey, carried out in 1986, only confirmed that the site belongs to the Púchov culture and that its chronological placing corresponds to the turn of the eras. Because of the severe disturbance of the site, three further surveys were carried out, including the use of a metal detector, which brought the decisive finds for a more precise dating of the fort. The first took place as early as 4 October 1998 and the other two on 11 and 14 April 1999. While the first two were held with the participation of members of the club from Povážská Bystrica, the last one was held with the participation of staff of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra as well (K. Pieta and collaborators). Together they found more than 60 metal objects, above all iron arrowheads, knives and nails, but also fragments of hooked implements (háčkovky), various working tools and fragments of iron. Above all a bronze brooch of the Almgren 68 type, a small bronze phalera and two silver coins, one Celtic, of the so-called Nitra type, and a medieval one of John Zápolya of 1527. After the first two socketed arrowheads, found in 1979 and 1986, a further 18 pieces of various types were discovered, which represent a wide range of forms and sizes of the arrowheads of the Púchov culture. Similar forms of arrowhead also appeared at the site of Skala at Púchov during the excavations of Baron Emil Hoening. Flat arrowheads with lateral barbs and without a socket are among the simplest long-range projectile weapons. The second type is arrowheads with a socket and two barbs. The third type is arrowheads with a socket and a single barb, and then there are also arrowheads with a flat, triangular point, or types of arrowhead with the point forged into an angular tip. All the types are also represented among the finds from the site of Skala at Púchov. Karol Pieta divided them into three basic groups: I – triangular points; II – leaf-shaped points; III – conical points. The first type is among the oldest forms of arrowhead made of iron sheet with the help of a chisel. The oldest of them have no socket and were set into the split end of the arrow. They belong to ancient forms with a simple production technique and appear as early as the Early Iron Age and in the earlier phase of the Late Iron Age. They survived also at the end of the Late Iron Age and the beginning of the Roman period as emergency products alongside the socketed forms, which required a more demanding production process.

Another relatively frequent find is iron nails and large wedges. Several pieces of them were found at the fort at Jasenica. They are among the frequent finds at the fortifications of the Púchov culture, although it is at present very difficult to determine on which implements, objects or structural fittings they were actually used. Perhaps only the large wedges may be regarded as part of dwelling or fortification structures.

Among the interesting objects from the site of Predná hôrka one may class the so-called háčkovky (hooked implements). They have been found at several fortifications of the Púchov culture, for example Prosné, Zlatý kôň, Udiča and Klapy, but their use is at present not sufficiently attested. Only certain hints can be deduced from their shapes and sizes – they have one end bent into a hook, a twisted body, and their relatively small dimensions allow no other possibility of use than for knitting yarn. Their possible use as small keys is hard to interpret because of their delicate form.

Among the important finds is also a fragment of a mirror, which was made of white metal. Similar fragments come from Divinka and Liptovská Mara. Unfortunately, in neither case was it possible to find a complete piece, and so on the basis of the reconstruction of these fragments it can only be assumed that their diameters reached about 8–10 cm. Almost unidentifiable are the various iron fragments which are hard to assign to particular specific objects. One find may perhaps be regarded as a small razor and another fragment as the point of an awl. Relatively rare is the find of a lead seal, which need not belong within the framework of the Púchov culture. The iron six-armed rosette also falls outside the overall framework; it may come from a medieval spur, but also from horse harness within the framework of the Púchov culture. Among the common finds, however, one may certainly class the iron knives which are often found at many sites of the Púchov culture. Out of the overall range of various types of knife, a large knife of sickle-like shape with a handle ending in an eyelet stands out. Similar or very closely related examples have also appeared at the upland settlement at Udiča in the locality of Klapy, or at Púchov at the site of Skala, which by its shape and dimensions is a very close analogy to the find from Jasenica. Very closely related knives – cleavers – have been found at Liptovská Mara but also at the fortification of Čertova skala at Trenčianske Teplice. Already in the Late Bronze Age related knives appear in central Europe which have their models among bronze examples, in a far more perfect form, in the so-called bird-shaped or leech-shaped bronze knives at various sites in Europe. Whether the finds from Jasenica, Púchov and Udiča too can be assigned to these cult objects is for the time being an open question. But in view of the not even very distant sacrificial site at Prosné in the locality of Uhliská, where sacrifices of animals and also of people took place in the late La Tène period, it need not be improbable.

Those who performed the sacrificial offerings held a more important position in the society of the time, and it is therefore possible to assume that such knives, which by their shape and dimensions stood out from the ordinary type of knife of the Púchov culture, could also have been a symbol precisely of the important members of the clan, those oriented towards performing sacrifices to the deities of the time. The sacrifices were often quartered, divided into smaller parts, which were carried out onto the fields or burnt on sacrificial fires.

Among the most important finds, from the point of view of the possibility of a more precise dating of the fortification at Jasenica in the locality of Predná hôrka, are two brooches. While the first is made of iron and, by the surviving part of its bow, resembles the derivatives of the Nauheim brooches, which represent the earlier horizon of the development of the Púchov culture within the late La Tène period, the second brooch is made of bronze and is among the relatively frequent finds in northern Slovakia. It can be classed among the bronze brooches of the Almgren type. These are among the most widespread types of fastener of the Early Roman period in the territory of Slovakia. Accordingly, it might perhaps be assumed that the occupation at the Predná hôrka fortification lasted longer than has hitherto been supposed and could have survived even to the middle of the 1st century AD. It evidently did not end at the beginning of that century, as might have been expected on the basis of the earlier finds.

Among the interesting finds from this site is also an iron key, which by its shape corresponds to similar finds from Liptovská Mara. Keys do not occur at the fortifications of the Púchov culture as often as other antiquities, but nevertheless the finds mentioned already speak of a different kind of securing of property than was the case in the preceding periods. At Skala at Púchov even more perfect variants were found, made not only of iron but also of bronze.

Because some finds from the site of Predná hôrka at Jasenica are later (medieval) than the main content of the body of finds, it was only a matter of time before this would be confirmed by irrefutable proof as well. That happened during the last survey on 14 April 1999, when a silver coin of King John Zápolya (1526 - 1540) of 1527, struck at Kremnica, was found.

The very most valuable find at the Predná hôrka fort was, after all, the silver coin of the so-called Nitra type, which was found on the southern slope of the site at a depth of about 10–15 cm. The coin is very well preserved (a tetradrachm), has a diameter of 24 mm and a weight of 9.985 g. On the obverse is the stylised body of a horse facing left; above its back and beneath its belly there is an irregular square symbol. The lower sign perhaps recalls a lyre? On the reverse is an animal that cannot be precisely identified – a dog? – turned to the right, which has an irregular line beneath its feet and above its back a pseudo-inscription enclosed between two straight lines. The edge of the coin on both sides is bordered by a coarse beaded pattern. The coin belongs to variant V/12 of the Nitra type.

Coins of this type are remarkable above all in that they no longer have a head depicted on the obverse, as is usual throughout Celtic coinage, but an animal is represented on both the obverse and the reverse. It may be supposed that the model for the image of the dog on the reverse was provided by Roman Republican coins – the denarii of C. Postumius of the years 74–73 BC, or of T. Carisius of 45 BC. These thus in fact contribute to the dating of the coins of the Nitra type to the second half of the 1st century BC. So far none of the 14 pieces of coin of this type has been precisely localised. The find from Jasenica is therefore the first with an unambiguous localisation, and it seems that a further example has been added from Skalka nad Váhom, which, however, has not so far been made available for study. Both of these precisely localised finds confirm that this type of coin was most probably struck in northern Slovakia (north-western?), and not in the Nitra area, as its name suggests. This is confirmed at the same time by the fact that one of the long-known coins of the Nitra type is in fact an overstrike on a tetradrachm of the northern Slovak Veľký Bysterec type. The find of the silver Celtic coin, dated to the period after 45 BC, also makes it possible to shift the building of the fortification on Predná hôrka at Jasenica deeper into the period of the 1st century BC than has hitherto been supposed. Its use perhaps lasted longer than the original finds, known from the previous surveys, attested.
